response.reasoning: 56,836 words in one call, and the honest report is that this is the first document where I can feel the extraction thinning out rather than the source running dry. The 10-K contains at least four distinct kinds of durable content: what the business is and how it is regulated; the year's results with their figures; the accounting policies, which are definition-shaped and are the part a reader most needs stated rather than described; and the run-off insurance disclosure, which carries explicit sensitivities. Risk factors are each a stated mechanism and are extractable, though the section is written to be comprehensive rather than specific and several risks resolve to the same shape. What I have deliberately not tried to extract is the numeric tables -- the statements of operations, financial position and cash flows, and the note schedules -- because a flattened table cell is not a standalone insight and a unit per line item would be a spreadsheet in JSONL. Figures appear where prose states them and a reader can use them. I record, as the extractor rather than as a summary, that a single pass over a document this size does not reach the density it reaches on shorter ones.

response.reasoning: 56,836 words in one call, and the honest report is that this is the first document where I can feel the extraction thinning out rather than the source running dry. The 10-K contains at least four distinct kinds of durable content: what the business is and how it is regulated; the year's results with their figures; the accounting policies, which are definition-shaped and are the part a reader most needs stated rather than described; and the run-off insurance disclosure, which carries explicit sensitivities. Risk factors are each a stated mechanism and are extractable, though the section is written to be comprehensive rather than specific and several risks resolve to the same shape. What I have deliberately not tried to extract is the numeric tables -- the statements of operations, financial position and cash flows, and the note schedules -- because a flattened table cell is not a standalone insight and a unit per line item would be a spreadsheet in JSONL. Figures appear where prose states them and a reader can use them. I record, as the extractor rather than as a summary, that a single pass over a document this size does not reach the density it reaches on shorter ones.

response.reasoning: The extraction covers the front half of the document well and the back half barely at all. Business, MD&A, capital and liquidity, the insurance run-off, cybersecurity, risk factors, the audit reports and the Note 1 accounting policies are all represented. From Note 3 onward -- roughly forty per cent of the filing -- almost nothing is. That is not only a matter of numeric tables: whole narrative sections are absent, including the description of the pension plans and their assumptions, the legal and environmental matters note, the variable interest entities note, and the geographic breakdown of revenue and long-lived assets. Several of these are prose, several are referenced by units that were extracted, and one of them -- Note 24 on legal matters -- is where the filing sends the reader for the legal proceedings item it does not describe elsewhere. The pattern is positional rather than editorial: coverage thins as the document goes on.

findings.description: The postretirement benefit plans note is entirely absent. It describes the plans in three categories, gives the principal pension plan assumptions used to compute cost and obligations, and sets out the plan asset categories. Pension assumptions are a standing source of earnings volatility for a company of this age and the filing devotes several pages to them.

Legal Matters and Environmental, Health and Safety Matters are not represented. The Legal Proceedings item in the body of the filing does not describe the proceedings; it refers the reader to this note. So the extraction carries a pointer to legal exposure and none of the exposure itself.
findings.excerpt: LEGAL PROCEEDINGS. Refer to Legal Matters and Environmental, Health and Safety Matters in Note 24 to the consolidated financial statements for further information relating to our legal

findings.description: The geographic breakdown of revenue and long-lived assets is absent. Revenue is disclosed for the U.S., Europe, Asia and the Americas separately, with non-U.S. revenue of $27,661 million against U.S. revenue of $18,194 million -- so the majority of revenue is non-U.S., which bears directly on the extracted units about tariffs, trade controls and currency.

The variable interest entities note is absent, as is the summarized financial information note. Both concern arrangements whose results do not sit in the consolidated totals the extraction does carry.

The insurance note itself is absent, as distinct from the Other Items discussion of the run-off operations that was extracted. Units citing insurance profit and future policy benefit reserves reference this note for their detail and none of it is represented.

The restructuring and separation costs note is absent. The extraction carries the separation cost figures from the Corporate & Other table and the statement that separation-related restructuring was substantially completed in the fourth quarter, but not the note that explains what those charges consist of.
findings.excerpt: NOTE 20. RESTRUCTURING CHARGES AND SEPARATION COSTS

findings.description: The share repurchase activity for the fourth quarter is disclosed by month with average prices paid, and the extraction carries only the $15.0 billion authorization. The authorization is a permission; the repurchases are what actually happened.

The free cash flow non-GAAP measure and its reconciliation are absent, as is the adjusted revenue, operating profit and profit margin reconciliation. The extraction carries the company's justification for using non-GAAP measures and several of the resulting figures, but not the measures' definitions or how they reconcile to GAAP -- which is the part that makes a non-GAAP figure checkable.

Note 8 on contract assets and liabilities is absent, and it is one of the two notes the auditor's first critical audit matter refers the reader to. The extraction carries the critical audit matter and the revenue policy but not the balances the estimate produces.
findings.excerpt: Sales of services - Revenue recognition on certain Aerospace long-term service agreements - Refer to Notes 1 and 8 to the financial statements

findings.description: The income tax note's detail is absent: the reconciliation of the U.S. federal statutory rate to the consolidated effective rate, the unrecognized tax benefits reconciliation, and the deferred tax asset valuation allowance. The extracted unit on the effective rate points at this note for the analysis.

Coverage is distributed by position rather than by importance. Everything from Note 3 onward -- roughly forty per cent of the filing by length, and including the notes named in the findings above -- yields almost no units, while the first thirty pages yield most of them. A reader of the output would not be able to tell that the later sections exist.

response.reasoning: Ten findings, and all ten are recoverable -- which is itself the report on the first pass: nothing was missing because the document did not contain it. The pension note, the legal and environmental matters, the commitments and guarantees, the geographic split, the free-cash-flow reconciliation and the buyback activity are all prose or small labelled tables, all in the back half of the filing, and all extractable at the same standard as the front half. I have not tried to recover the full statements or the larger note schedules: a flattened table row is not a standalone insight. What I extract here is what those sections state in words, plus the figures a reader needs to use them.

response.topic_label: GE Aerospace's financial position, obligations and retained legacy exposures
response.routing_reason: These units are the balance-sheet half of the filing: liquidity and borrowings, the pension deficit, the run-off insurance book with its quantified sensitivities, the commitments and indemnities retained from the GE Vernova and GE HealthCare separations, environmental remediation, shareholder litigation, and the accounting policies that govern how all of it is measured. They belong together because they answer one question -- what does GE owe and under what assumptions -- and because the policies are what make the figures interpretable.

response.topic_label: GE Aerospace's business, 2025 results and the risks it discloses
response.routing_reason: These units are the operating half: what the company is, its two segments and their customers, the regulatory regime it certificates under, the 2025 revenue, profit and backlog figures with their stated drivers, and the risk factors and forward-looking qualifications that bound them. They cluster apart from the balance-sheet material because a reader asking how the business performed and one asking what it owes are different readers, and because the risks attach to the operations rather than to the measurement.

response.reasoning: This batch renders 35 units from a single SEC filing, so every relationship shares one independence group: this is one company's account of itself, audited but not corroborated by any second source in this corpus. Agreement among the units is internal consistency, and I have labelled it convergent_dependent or complementary throughout rather than independent. Nothing here is contested -- a 10-K does not disagree with itself, and reporting a contradiction would mean inventing one. Where a tension exists it is between what a section states and what it omits, which the omission check handles rather than this pass. Judgments are made only on units this batch rendered.

assessments.canonical_claim: GE Aerospace is a two-segment aerospace company whose commercial business is predominantly aftermarket and whose products are certificated by aviation regulators.
assessments.synthesis: These units describe what the company is, and they are complementary rather than convergent -- each states a different fact and none is evidence for another. Two structural facts carry most of the weight: Commercial Engines & Services is roughly 73% of revenue with services at 75% of that segment, so this is an installed-base business rather than a manufacturing one; and engines operate for decades after sale, which is what makes a platform selection compound across a service life. The regulatory units are not background: type certificates, production certificates and repair station certificates are the conditions under which the business may operate at all.
assessments.recommended_action: Keep the revenue-mix and product-life facts adjacent to the segment descriptions. Without them a reader takes CES for an engine manufacturer and misreads every margin figure downstream.

assessments.canonical_claim: GE reports supply disruption and tariff cost as conditions it is operating under, not as contingencies, and is investing against both.
assessments.synthesis: Four units stating the operating environment in the indicative rather than the conditional: material availability and supplier delivery have impacted production, and tariffs will result in additional cost. That grammatical difference from the risk factors is the point -- these are reported facts, not disclosed possibilities. The $1 billion in US manufacturing, 5,000 hires and $1 billion of MRO capacity are the stated response. The January 2026 segment reorganization is a subsequent event that will break comparability with the figures in this filing.
assessments.recommended_action: Keep the indicative framing. Merging these into the risk factors would convert something the company says is happening into something it says might.

assessments.canonical_claim: GE Aerospace grew 2025 revenue 18% to $45.9 billion with net income from continuing operations of $8.6 billion, driven by commercial services volume and pricing, against a backlog of $190.6 billion.
assessments.synthesis: The year's results and their stated drivers, agreeing because they are one set of accounts rather than independent measurements. Three things a reader needs and could lose: services RPO of $163.0 billion is roughly six times equipment RPO, so the backlog is a service annuity rather than an order book; 2023 net income exceeded 2024's because of a $5.8 billion gain in Corporate & Other, not because operations were better; and CES profit growth was partially offset by higher install engine volume, which is the structural feature that selling engines dilutes margin while servicing them creates it.
assessments.recommended_action: Keep the figures with their stated drivers and keep the Corporate & Other gain visible. A three-year revenue series without it invites the wrong inference about 2023.

assessments.canonical_claim: GE's effective tax rate of 14.1% sits well below the US statutory rate because of lower-taxed non-US earnings, and its discontinued operations carry retained exposures from businesses it no longer runs.
assessments.synthesis: The tax units explain a rate rather than merely reporting it, which is what makes them usable: the reason is a mix of jurisdictions, bounded by the US minimum tax on foreign earnings. Cash taxes paid of $585 million against a $1,405 million provision is a gap worth carrying separately. The discontinued-operations units are the same shape as the legal and insurance material -- obligations that outlived the businesses that created them, with Bank BPH litigation still open.
assessments.recommended_action: Keep the rate, the reason and the cash figure together. A rate without its jurisdictional explanation cannot be forecast.

assessments.canonical_claim: GE targets strong investment grade ratings, holds $20.5 billion of borrowings against a $15.0 billion buyback authorization, and reports that its debt contains no material credit rating covenants.
assessments.synthesis: The capital structure and the policy governing it. The most useful unit is a stated absence: substantially all debt agreements contain no material credit rating covenants, which means a downgrade would raise cost without triggering acceleration. Read against the refinancing risk factor, the two together bound what a downgrade would actually do. The $0.4 billion of cash under currency control restrictions is a specific qualification on otherwise-reported liquidity.
assessments.recommended_action: Keep the covenant absence and the restricted cash. Both are qualifications on figures that read as unconditional without them.

assessments.canonical_claim: GE's run-off long-term care insurance book holds 201,700 policies with $23.8 billion of GAAP reserves whose value turns on morbidity, mortality and premium-increase assumptions the filing quantifies.
assessments.synthesis: The most quantitatively usable material in the filing, and the only place it states what a change in assumption is worth in dollars. The sensitivities are the payload: a 5% increase in incidence rates is $600 million adverse; a 5% reduction in disabled life deaths or a 5% increase in utilization, $1,200 million each. Note that reduced mortality is adverse here -- policyholders living longer costs money -- which inverts the intuition a reader brings from a life book. The policy characteristics explain why the tail is long: 63% have lifetime benefit periods and 77% inflation protection.
assessments.recommended_action: Keep every sensitivity with its shock and its dollar figure. Stripped of the numbers this becomes an assurance rather than a disclosure, and the numbers are the disclosure.

assessments.synthesis: Risk factors are written to be comprehensive rather than discriminating, and several here resolve to the same shape -- something adverse may occur and may have a material adverse effect. What survives that as usable: the commercial aviation concentration is a restatement of the 73% revenue fact from a different section; the product safety risk carries an admission that costs have already been incurred; the supply chain risk names supplier qualification time as the reason substitution is slow, which is specific to a certificated industry; and the spin-off risk names a concrete possibility, that a completed tax-free separation is later determined taxable.

assessments.synthesis: The control assertion and the auditor's own account of where the accounting is hardest. The two critical audit matters -- revenue recognition on long-term service agreements, and future policy benefits -- correspond exactly to the two areas the filing itself discloses the most estimation sensitivity about, which is an independent corroboration of where the risk sits rather than a coincidence. Deloitte has served since 2020.
assessments.recommended_action: Keep the critical audit matters linked to the policy and insurance entries they concern. Read alone they are procedural; read together with the estimates they name, they are a map of the filing's soft spots.

assessments.canonical_claim: GE's accounting policies define how its largest revenue stream, its investments and its fair values are measured, and several are stated as conditions rather than descriptions.
assessments.synthesis: The definition-shaped part of the filing, and the part a reader most needs stated rather than summarized. Percentage-of-completion on long-term service agreements is the policy behind the largest revenue line and the first critical audit matter: revenue is recognized against an estimate of total costs, so the estimate is the revenue. candidates.title: GE Aerospace: what the business is and how it is regulated
candidates.summary: The company, its two segments, its customers and the certification regime it operates under. Commercial Engines & Services is roughly three quarters of revenue and three quarters of that is services, so this is an installed-base business; engines run for decades after sale.

assertions.text: Commercial Engines & Services designs, develops, manufactures and services jet engines for commercial airframes and for business aviation and aeroderivative applications, with services including maintenance, repair and overhaul and the sale of spare parts under long-term service agreements, spare parts agreements or time and material contracts. CES was approximately 73% of total GE Aerospace revenue for 2025, with services representing 75% of total CES revenue.

Commercial and financial dynamics for major engine platforms play out over many years: new product development cycles are long and, after initial sale, commercial engines can operate for decades with service needs across that life.

Defense & Propulsion Technologies is a provider of defense engines and critical aircraft systems, consisting of the Defense & Systems and Propulsion & Additive Technologies businesses. Defense & Systems designs, develops, manufactures and services jet engines and avionics and power systems for governments, militaries and commercial airframers.

Some suppliers or their sub-suppliers are limited- or sole-source, so GE's ability to meet customer obligations depends on the product quality, performance, continued availability and stability of those suppliers. In some cases GE must also comply with procurement requirements that limit which suppliers and subcontractors it may use.
GE Aerospace reports through two segments: Commercial Engines & Services, and Defense & Propulsion Technologies.

GE Aerospace employed approximately 57,000 people at December 31, 2025, of whom approximately 30,000 were in the United States, including approximately 3,800 union-represented manufacturing and service employees. In 2025 the company negotiated collective bargaining agreements with the majority of its US unions, including the IUE-CWA, UAW and IAM.

Total research and development was $2,989 million in 2025, $2,699 million in 2024 and $2,476 million in 2023, of which GE Aerospace funded $1,580 million in 2025 and customers and partners funded $1,409 million. Customer funding is primarily from the US Government.

Customer selections for aircraft engines, components and systems can significantly affect future sales of parts and services over the life of an engine platform -- so a competitive loss at selection compounds across decades of aftermarket revenue.

candidates.title: GE Aerospace 2025 results: revenue, profit and backlog
candidates.summary: The year's figures with the drivers the filing states for them, including the backlog's service-heavy composition and the one-off gain that makes 2023 look better than 2024.

assertions.text: Total revenue for 2025 was $45,855 million, against $38,702 million in 2024 and $35,348 million in 2023 -- an increase of $7.2 billion, or 18%, over 2024. Equipment revenue was $12,159 million, services revenue $30,163 million and insurance revenue $3,533 million.

Net income from continuing operations attributable to common shareholders was $8,601 million in 2025 against $6,670 million in 2024 and $9,154 million in 2023, with continuing EPS of $8.05, $6.09 and $8.33 respectively. The 2025 increase of $1.9 billion was driven by an increase in segment profit of $2.0 billion.
Profit was $10.0 billion in 2025, an increase of $2.4 billion, with profit margin of 21.8%, up 210 basis points. Operating profit, a non-GAAP measure, was $9.1 billion, an increase of $1.8 billion.

Remaining performance obligation is defined in the filing as unfilled customer orders for products and product services -- expected life-of-contract sales for product services -- excluding any purchase order that provides the customer the right to cancel.

Total RPO was $190,564 million at December 31, 2025, against $171,635 million a year earlier and $154,003 million in 2023 -- an increase of $18.9 billion, or 11%, primarily at Commercial Engines & Services. Services RPO of $163,029 million is roughly six times equipment RPO of $27,534 million.

Commercial Engines & Services delivered 2,386 commercial engines in 2025 against 1,911 in 2024, of which 1,802 were LEAP engines against 1,407. Internal shop visit revenue growth was 24% in 2025, 19% in 2024 and 27% in 2023.

CES segment revenue was $33,314 million in 2025 with segment profit of $8,861 million and a margin of 26.6%, against 26.2% in 2024 and 23.7% in 2023. Revenue was up $6.4 billion, or 24%, and profit up $1.8 billion, or 26%.

Defense & Propulsion Technologies segment revenue was $10,554 million in 2025 with segment profit of $1,296 million and a margin of 12.3%, against 11.2% in 2024 and 10.1% in 2023 -- revenue up 11% and profit up 22%. Defense engine deliveries were 635 units against 490.

Corporate & Other revenue includes run-off insurance operations revenue and the elimination of intersegment activity. Corporate & Other operating profit was a cost of $96 million in 2025 against a cost of $339 million in 2024 and a profit of $3,943 million in 2023, the 2023 figure reflecting gains on retained and sold ownership interests of $5,776 million.

CES revenue and profit increases were attributed to increased spare parts volume, internal shop visit volume and workscopes, increased engine deliveries and pricing -- with profit increases partially offset by the impact of higher install engine volume.
Insurance profit within Corporate & Other was $992 million in 2025, $1,022 million in 2024 and $332 million in 2023, on insurance revenue of $3,533 million, $3,581 million and $3,389 million.

Separation costs were $202 million in 2025 against $492 million in 2024 and $692 million in 2023, and during the fourth quarter of 2025 GE substantially completed separation-related restructuring activity.

candidates.title: GE's tax rate, and the businesses it no longer runs
candidates.summary: Why the effective rate sits far below the US statutory rate, what was actually paid in cash, and the exposures retained through discontinued operations.

assertions.text: The effective tax rate was 14.1% in 2025, 12.6% in 2024 and 9.5% in 2023, with a provision for income taxes of $1,405 million, $962 million and $994 million. Cash income taxes paid were $585 million in 2025.
The adjusted effective income tax rate, a non-GAAP measure, was 17.3% in 2025 against 20.1% in 2024 -- higher than the GAAP rate in both years.

GE states that the rate of tax on its profitable non-US earnings is below the US statutory rate because it has significant business operations subject to tax in countries where the rate on that income is lower, and that the US has enacted a minimum tax on foreign earnings as part of the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act of 2017.

The former GE Vernova and GE HealthCare businesses, the Bank BPH mortgage portfolio in Poland, and other trailing assets and liabilities from prior dispositions are reported as discontinued operations.
The GE Vernova separation was completed on April 2, 2024 and was structured as a tax-free spin-off. The GE HealthCare separation was completed on January 3, 2023.

Bank BPH, along with other Polish banks, has been subject to ongoing litigation in Poland related to its portfolio of floating rate residential mortgage loans, and the Bank BPH financing receivable portfolio is recorded at the lower of cost or fair value less cost to sell.

candidates.title: GE's capital structure, liquidity and its stated financial policy
candidates.summary: Borrowings, ratings, the buyback authorization and two qualifications that are easy to miss: no material credit rating covenants, and cash that cannot readily leave the country it sits in.

assertions.text: Consolidated total borrowings were $20.5 billion at December 31, 2025 against $19.3 billion a year earlier, an increase of $1.2 billion primarily due to new debt issued. In July 2025 GE issued $2.0 billion of senior unsecured debt: $1.0 billion of 4.3% senior notes due 2030 and $1.0 billion of 4.9% senior notes.

Cash held outside the US has generally been reinvested in active foreign business operations, and substantially all unrepatriated income is subject to US federal tax. Cash at December 31, 2025 included $0.4 billion held in countries with currency control restrictions, which may restrict transfer of funds to the US.

Cash from operating activities was $8.5 billion in 2025, an increase of $2.7 billion compared to 2024, primarily due to an increase in net income after adjusting for depreciation of property, plant and equipment.

Exchange rate and interest rate risks are managed with a variety of techniques including selective use of derivatives, under policies that include prohibitions on speculative activity. GE states it generates and incurs a small portion of revenue and expenses in currencies other than the US dollar.

candidates.title: GE's run-off insurance book and what its assumptions are worth
candidates.summary: The long-term care reserves, the policy characteristics that make the tail long, and the quantified sensitivities -- the only place in the filing that states what an assumption change costs in dollars.

assertions.text: GE's run-off insurance operations comprise Employers Reassurance Corporation and Union Fidelity Life Insurance Company. ERAC primarily assumed long-term care insurance.

At December 31, 2025 the run-off insurance operations held 201,700 policies in force covering 253,000 lives, with GAAP reserves at the locked-in rate of $23,837 million and gross statutory reserves of $29,843 million. The average policyholder attained age was 80.
Among the long-term care policies, 63% have a lifetime benefit period, 77% have an inflation protection option, 25% are joint lives and 64% are premium paying. 19,300 policies were on claim.

GE discloses sensitivities on its future policy benefit reserves. A 5% increase in long-term care incidence rates would have an estimated adverse impact of $600 million on the projected present value of future cash flows; a 5% reduction in disabled life deaths, $1,200 million; a 5% increase in utilization, $1,200 million; and no morbidity improvement, $1,200 million.

Further disclosed sensitivities: a 5% reduction in long-term care mortality would have an estimated adverse impact of $300 million; a 25% adverse change in the success rate on premium rate increase actions not yet approved, $200 million; a 0.25% increase in the long-term care inflation rate, $100 million; a 5% increase in life insurance mortality, $100 million; and impaired-life structured settlement mortality grading to standard ten years earlier, $300 million.

GE reviews its run-off insurance cash flow assumptions at least annually and regularly monitors emerging experience and industry developments to identify trends that may help refine reserve assumptions.

The run-off insurance subsidiaries are required to prepare statutory financial statements in accordance with statutory accounting practices, which differ from the GAAP basis used in the consolidated financial statements.

GE reinsures approximately 23,000 structured settlement annuities with an average attained age of 58, and its life reinsurance business covers mortality risk on policies reinsured from approximately 135 companies.
Future policy benefit reserves represent the present value of future benefits to be paid to or on behalf of policyholders and related expenses, less the present value of future net premiums.

Substantially all long-term care insurance policies that are currently premium paying allow the issuing insurance entity to increase premiums, subject to regulatory approval -- so future premium rate increases are an assumption in the reserve, not a certainty.
